text:
I grew up living in what I considered an urban environment. But when I moved to the other side of the country, I realized just how many trees they had. And I realized I hadn't appreciated the trees where I was growing up. I think it's the same as a lot of us. We don't appreciate the trees because they're everywhere, or they're not there. But in an urban environment, trees are infrastructure. They are so much more than decorative. I think we need to really make it a priority for our cities to have trees, to grow trees. They should not be an amenity. They should be infrastructure. So we need to start building our urban forests. And that's the conversation that I'm excited about. And I think it's a very urgent conversation.
And in terms of the environmental benefits, trees cool us. They provide shade. And if you're in a concrete city or an asphalt city, the urban heat island effect can really warm up the city. And it can be several degrees. And trees will help cool it down. And they do that in multiple ways. They provide shade, so they cool the surface. And they also cool the air. So it's a multi-faceted benefit. And it helps us to avoid heat-related illnesses and even deaths. And then trees help us with air quality. They filter particulate matter, they absorb carbon dioxide, they release oxygen, etc. And they help with water management. Their roots and leaves capture water, and that reduces flooding and eases the burden on our stormwater infrastructure. And we're seeing more extreme weather events, so we're seeing more extreme precipitation events. And so trees help us deal with that. So that's the environmental benefit, which is the most urgent.
But then beyond that, there are benefits to our mental health, to our physical health, to our sense of well-being. And there's a lot of research on that. And I think there's a lot of research showing that access to green space helps reduce stress, helps with concentration, helps with mental health. And for kids, it's great to have places to play and to explore. And for adults, it's nice to have a walk under a canopy. And it can lower blood pressure, it can restore attention, etc. And for hospitals, it's been shown that hospitals that have views of trees, patients recover faster, they need less pain medication, etc. And so it's really good for our health. And I think in a society where we're realizing the cost of loneliness, the cost of being sedentary, etc., it's really good to have that free, public, therapeutic benefit that trees provide.
And then there's community benefits. Trees help bring community. If a neighborhood has good trees, people spend more time outdoors. They look out for each other. They walk around. And so it can really help with crime. And there are economic benefits, too. If you have a neighborhood with good trees, property values go up. And if you have a good tree canopy, it makes the neighborhood more walkable, it makes people less reliant on cars, it helps with public transit, it helps with local businesses. And so it helps the local economy. And then there's an equity component, because the places that have the least trees, the places that are the most urbanized, the places that have the most pollution, the places that have the most heat, those are often the low-income neighborhoods. And so it's really important that we plant trees equitably and make sure that the places that need them the most are the places that we're planting them. And that's really, really important.
But the challenges are, planting trees is hard. It costs money. It takes a lot of water. It takes a lot of maintenance. If you plant a young tree and don't take care of it, it will die. And if you plant the wrong species, it can be a problem. It can crack sidewalks, it can block views, it can worsen allergies. And people worry that if we put trees in, it will increase rents and displace people. And that's a real phenomenon called green gentrification. And so we need to be mindful of that. And we need to be mindful of all these things. And we need to have community engagement, we need to have the right species, we need to have the right maintenance, we need to have the right planning. But it's not a reason to not do it. It's a reason to do it well. And the alternative of having a city with no trees is much worse. And so I think it's worth it. And I think we should be investing in trees as a priority. And I think it's really important to think about it as infrastructure, not as an amenity.
